templates.title: One query, then many
templates.prompt: This endpoint returns posts with their authors. It works and the tests pass. Explain what is wrong with it and what that costs at scale.
templates.objective: Recognize an N+1 query pattern hidden inside an ordinary-looking loop.
hints: Count how many database round trips happen for a page of 100 posts.
Look closely at what is being awaited inside the loop.
templates.explanation: The loop body awaits a database call, so each iteration is a separate round trip. The query count scales with the result set rather than staying constant. Either join the author in the original query or collect the author ids and fetch them in one findMany, then map them in memory.

answerKey.flaw: The author is fetched inside the loop, so the endpoint issues one query per post instead of one query for all of them — a classic N+1.
answerKey.consequence: Latency grows linearly with the page size and the database sees limit+1 round trips per request. At limit=100 this is 101 queries where 2 would do. Fix it with an include/join or a single findMany over the collected author ids.

goodAnswerSignals: Explains that query count scales with page size
weakAnswerSignals: Says the code looks correct
Only suggests adding an index
followUpPrompts: How would you rewrite this with a single query?
mayaPushbacks: How many queries run when limit is 100?

templates.title: A cache that only grows
templates.prompt: This memoizes an expensive lookup. It is correct and it is fast. Explain what is wrong with it and what that costs in production.
templates.objective: Spot a memoization cache with no eviction policy and no expiry.
hints: Consider what happens after a million distinct users have been requested.
Ask what happens when a profile is updated somewhere else.
templates.explanation: A Map used as a cache holds a strong reference to every key it has ever seen. Without a maximum size, a TTL, or invalidation on update, it is a memory leak that also serves stale data. Bound it with an LRU and expire entries, and clear the key when the underlying profile changes.

answerKey.flaw: Entries are added but never evicted and never expire, so the cache grows without bound and serves stale profiles forever.
answerKey.consequence: Memory grows with the number of distinct users the process ever sees, ending in an out-of-memory restart on a long-lived server. Separately, a profile updated elsewhere is never reflected. Needs a size bound or a TTL, and invalidation on write.

goodAnswerSignals: Names unbounded growth or the missing eviction policy
Mentions staleness as well as memory
weakAnswerSignals: Praises the caching without noting the growth
Suggests only a bigger machine
followUpPrompts: What eviction policy would you pick here, and why?
mayaPushbacks: When does an entry ever leave this cache?

templates.title: The promise nobody waited for
templates.prompt: This handler records an audit entry before returning. Explain what is wrong with it and what that costs in production.
templates.objective: Identify a floating promise whose failure is invisible and whose completion is not guaranteed.
hints: Compare how the two database calls in this function are invoked.
Ask what happens if the second write rejects.
templates.explanation: An async call without await returns a promise that nobody observes. The handler responds immediately, so the audit write races the end of the request, and if it rejects there is no catch anywhere — an unhandled rejection. Either await it, or attach a catch and document that the write is intentionally fire-and-forget.

answerKey.flaw: The audit write is not awaited, so the response can be sent before it completes and any rejection becomes an unhandled promise rejection.
answerKey.consequence: Audit entries are silently lost when the process finishes the request first, and a failing write crashes the process on newer Node versions rather than surfacing as a handled error. Await it, or deliberately detach it with a catch handler and a comment saying why.

goodAnswerSignals: Mentions unhandled rejection or lost writes
weakAnswerSignals: Says both writes are awaited
Focuses only on input validation
followUpPrompts: When is fire-and-forget actually the right call here?
mayaPushbacks: What handles a rejection from the audit write?

templates.title: Read, think, overwrite
templates.prompt: This increments a view counter. It is correct when tested by one user. Explain what is wrong with it and what that costs under real traffic.
templates.objective: Recognize a lost-update race created by read-modify-write across two statements.
hints: Imagine two requests arriving at the same millisecond.
Ask what happens between the read and the write.
templates.explanation: Between the read and the write, another request can complete the same sequence. Both read the same starting value and both write value+1, so two views are recorded as one. The database can do this atomically — an increment expression, or a transaction with the right isolation — and application-side arithmetic on a shared counter is the bug.

answerKey.flaw: The counter is read and written in two separate statements, so concurrent calls read the same value and one increment overwrites the other.
answerKey.consequence: Under concurrent traffic the view count drifts permanently low, and the loss grows with concurrency. Use an atomic database increment rather than read-modify-write in application code.

goodAnswerSignals: Names the lost update or the read-modify-write race
weakAnswerSignals: Says it is fine because both statements are awaited
Suggests only adding an index
followUpPrompts: Would wrapping both statements in a transaction be enough?
mayaPushbacks: What guarantees nothing changes between the read and the write?

templates.title: Retry until it charges twice
templates.prompt: This retries a payment call on failure, which sounds prudent. Explain what is wrong with it and what that costs in production.
templates.objective: Recognize that retrying a non-idempotent operation can duplicate its side effect.
hints: A timeout means the response was lost, not that nothing happened.
Ask what makes the second attempt distinguishable from a new payment.
templates.explanation: A timeout tells you the response was lost, not that the work did not happen. Retrying a bare charge treats an ambiguous failure as a definite one. Generating a stable idempotency key before the first attempt and sending it on every retry lets the gateway recognize the duplicate and return the original result.

answerKey.flaw: The charge is retried without an idempotency key, so a request that actually succeeded but timed out is charged again on the retry.
answerKey.consequence: A network timeout after the gateway has already taken the money produces a duplicate charge — the retry has no way to say this is the same payment. Pass a stable idempotency key generated once, before the loop, so the gateway can deduplicate.

weakAnswerSignals: Says three retries is too many and stops there
Only suggests longer backoff
followUpPrompts: Where should the idempotency key be generated, and why there?
mayaPushbacks: What if the first charge succeeded but the response timed out?

templates.title: Awaited one at a time
templates.prompt: This gathers three independent pieces of data for a dashboard. Explain what is wrong with it and what that costs in production.
templates.objective: Spot independent async calls serialized by await when they could run concurrently.
hints: Check whether any of these three calls uses the result of another.
Add up the latency if each request takes 200 milliseconds.
templates.explanation: await suspends until each call finishes before the next one starts. Because no call uses the result of a previous one, the sequencing buys nothing and costs the sum of all three latencies. Promise.all starts them together and waits once, turning the sum into the maximum.

answerKey.flaw: Three independent requests are awaited sequentially, so the total latency is their sum rather than their maximum.
answerKey.consequence: A dashboard that could load in 200ms takes 600ms, and the gap widens as calls are added. None of the three depends on another, so they should start together with Promise.all.

weakAnswerSignals: Says await is required here
Suggests caching without addressing the sequencing
followUpPrompts: What changes if getUsage needs the profile id?
mayaPushbacks: Which of these three calls depends on another?

templates.title: A page that skips a row
templates.prompt: This paginates a list. The first page looks right. Explain what is wrong with it and what that costs in production.
templates.objective: Recognize that offset pagination needs a total ordering to be stable.
hints: Consider several rows written in the same millisecond.
Ask whether this ordering is guaranteed to be the same across two separate queries.
templates.explanation: Two rows with the same createdAt have no defined relative order, so the database may return them differently between queries. With skip/take, that means a row can be counted on page one and page two, or skipped by both. Ordering by createdAt and then id makes the sort total and the paging stable.

answerKey.flaw: Ordering is by a non-unique createdAt with no tie-breaker, so rows sharing a timestamp can appear on two pages or on none.
answerKey.consequence: Users see duplicated or silently missing items when several rows share a createdAt, and the bug is invisible in small test data. Add a unique tie-breaker such as id to make the ordering total, or switch to cursor pagination.

goodAnswerSignals: Proposes a tie-breaker or cursor pagination
weakAnswerSignals: Focuses only on the skip arithmetic
Says offset pagination is always fine
followUpPrompts: How does cursor pagination avoid this entirely?
mayaPushbacks: Is this ordering guaranteed to be identical across two queries?

templates.title: The listener that never leaves
templates.prompt: This React effect keeps a widget in sync with the window size. Explain what is wrong with it and what that costs in production.
templates.objective: Recognize an effect that acquires a subscription without releasing it.
hints: Ask what happens to the listener when this component unmounts.
Consider a user navigating to this screen ten times.
templates.explanation: An effect that subscribes must return a function that unsubscribes. Without it, the listener stays attached to window after the component unmounts, holding its closure and state setter alive. Navigating back and forth registers a new listener each time, so the leak compounds.

answerKey.flaw: The effect registers a resize listener and returns no cleanup, so the listener survives unmount and accumulates on every remount.
answerKey.consequence: Each mount adds another listener that keeps the component's closure alive, so memory grows and setWidth is eventually called on unmounted components. Return a cleanup that removes the listener.

templates.title: Errors that vanish in a loop
templates.prompt: This sends a notification to each recipient. Explain what is wrong with it and what that costs in production.
templates.objective: Recognize a reported result that does not reflect what actually happened.
hints: Ask where the returned count comes from.
Consider one recipient failing out of fifty.
templates.explanation: Promise.all rejects as soon as one promise rejects, so the function either throws or claims full success — there is no partial truth. The returned count is derived from the input length rather than from outcomes. Promise.allSettled gives each result, letting the function report how many actually sent and which recipients failed.

answerKey.flaw: The count returned assumes every send succeeded, and Promise.all rejects on the first failure so the remaining outcomes are never inspected.
answerKey.consequence: The caller is told every recipient was notified even when sends failed, and one failure discards the status of all the others. Use Promise.allSettled and report the real successes and failures.

templates.title: Filtered after the fact
templates.prompt: This returns a user's recent orders. It returns correct results. Explain what is wrong with it and what that costs at scale.

hints: Consider a table with ten million orders.

templates.explanation: The database is asked for every row, and the narrowing happens afterwards in JavaScript. templates.title: Two writes, no transaction
templates.prompt: This transfers credit between two accounts. Explain what is wrong with it and what that costs in production.
templates.objective: Recognize two related writes that must be atomic but are not.
hints: Ask what the balances look like if the process dies between the two updates.
Consider whether each statement being atomic makes the pair atomic.
templates.explanation: Each update is atomic on its own, which is not the same as the pair being atomic. A crash, timeout, or validation error between them leaves the system in a state no business rule allows. Running both inside db.$transaction makes the pair all-or-nothing.

answerKey.flaw: The debit and the credit are separate statements with no transaction, so a failure between them destroys money.
answerKey.consequence: If the second update fails or the process dies between the two, the amount is debited and never credited. Wrap both in a single transaction so they commit or roll back together.

templates.title: Deleted, but still counted

templates.title: Two hundred at once
templates.prompt: This resizes every uploaded image for a gallery. Explain what is wrong with it and what that costs in production.
templates.objective: Recognize Promise.all used as parallelism with no bound on the number in flight.
hints: Ask how many operations run at once for a gallery of two thousand.

templates.explanation: Promise.all waits for everything but starts everything immediately. The number in flight equals the input length, which is attacker- or user-controlled. A worker pool with a fixed size gives the same result with predictable resource use.

templates.title: The stale closure
templates.prompt: This autosaves a document every ten seconds. Explain what is wrong with it and what the user loses.
templates.objective: Recognize a long-lived callback closing over state that will not be updated.
hints: Ask which value of content the callback can see after ten minutes of typing.
Note that the cleanup is correct — the defect is elsewhere.
templates.explanation: The empty dependency array runs the effect once, so the closure passed to setInterval captures the first content value forever. Cleanup is present and correct, which makes the bug easy to miss. A ref updated on each render gives the interval access to current state without re-subscribing.

answerKey.flaw: The effect captures content once on mount and never re-subscribes, so the interval keeps saving the original value.
answerKey.consequence: Every autosave writes the document as it was when the screen opened, silently discarding everything typed since. Use a ref holding the latest value, or re-create the interval when content changes.

goodAnswerSignals: Proposes a ref or a corrected dependency
weakAnswerSignals: Says the cleanup is missing
Suggests a shorter interval
followUpPrompts: Why is adding content to the dependency array an imperfect fix?
mayaPushbacks: Which content does the interval save after ten minutes?

templates.title: Money in floats
templates.prompt: This totals a shopping cart. Explain what is wrong with it and what the user eventually sees.
templates.objective: Recognize currency arithmetic performed in a type that cannot represent it exactly.
hints: Try adding 0.1 and 0.2 in a JavaScript console.
Ask whether toFixed changes the stored value or only how it is shown.
templates.explanation: Binary floating point cannot represent most decimal fractions exactly, so repeated addition accumulates error. toFixed hides it at display time without fixing the stored value. Working in paise as integers makes every operation exact, converting to a decimal only for display.

answerKey.flaw: Currency is accumulated in binary floating point, so amounts like 0.1 and 0.2 do not sum exactly and the total drifts.
answerKey.consequence: Totals disagree with the sum of the line items by a paisa, and the discrepancy compounds across a large cart and reconciles badly against payment records. Store and add money as integer minor units.

weakAnswerSignals: Says toFixed solves it
Suggests rounding at each step
followUpPrompts: Where exactly would you convert back to rupees?
mayaPushbacks: Does toFixed fix the number or only its display?

templates.title: Sorted in place
templates.prompt: This renders a sorted view of a list held in state. Explain what is wrong with it.
templates.objective: Recognize an in-place array method applied to state or props.
hints: Check whether sort returns a new array or the same one.
Ask what else holds a reference to the tasks array.
templates.explanation: sort returns the same array it was given, having reordered it. Because tasks came from state, this rewrites state during render — an update React never observed. Spreading into a new array first keeps the render pure and leaves the source untouched.

answerKey.flaw: Array.sort mutates in place, so this reorders the caller's state array during render instead of producing a new list.
answerKey.consequence: Props are mutated during render, so React may not detect the change, other consumers of the same array see it reorder unexpectedly, and the render is no longer pure. Copy before sorting.

weakAnswerSignals: Says sort returns a new array
Focuses only on the key prop
followUpPrompts: Which other array methods have this property?
mayaPushbacks: Does sort copy the array first?

templates.title: Derived, then stored
templates.prompt: This keeps a formatted label alongside a value. Explain what is wrong with it and what the user sees.
templates.objective: Recognize state that duplicates something already derivable from props.
hints: Count how many renders happen when amount changes.
Ask what the effect is compensating for.
templates.explanation: useState initializes once, so the effect exists purely to re-synchronize. That means every change renders the old value, then the new one. Since format is a pure function of amount, calling it during render removes the state, the effect, the extra render and the possibility of drift.

answerKey.flaw: A value fully derivable from props is copied into state, so it renders stale for one frame after every change and can drift out of sync.
answerKey.consequence: Each amount change renders the previous label once before the effect corrects it, producing a visible flicker and an extra render. Compute the label during render instead of storing it.

goodAnswerSignals: Notes the extra render or flicker
weakAnswerSignals: Says the dependency array is wrong
Suggests useMemo without removing the state
followUpPrompts: When is copying a prop into state actually correct?
mayaPushbacks: What does the effect exist to fix?

templates.title: Counting the whole table
templates.prompt: This renders a paginated table with a total count. Explain what is wrong with it at scale.
templates.objective: Recognize an exact total that costs more than the data it accompanies.
hints: Compare the cost of fetching 50 rows against counting 50 million.
Ask which half of this Promise.all takes longer as the table grows.
templates.explanation: Counting all rows cannot use a covering index the way a limited read can; the database inspects the whole table. The fifty rows are cheap and the count is not, so the query that matters least dominates the latency. Most products can use an approximate total or omit the page count entirely.

answerKey.flaw: An unfiltered count runs on every page request, which scans the whole table rather than using an index.
answerKey.consequence: Once the table reaches tens of millions of rows, the count dominates the request and the page slows even though only fifty rows are returned. Cache the total, approximate it, or drop the exact page count.

goodAnswerSignals: Suggests caching, approximating or removing it
weakAnswerSignals: Says Promise.all makes it free
Suggests an index on the primary key
followUpPrompts: What would you show instead of an exact page count?
mayaPushbacks: Which of these two queries gets slower as the table grows?

templates.title: Deep pages get slower
templates.prompt: This powers an infinite scroll that users sometimes take very far. Explain what is wrong with it.
templates.objective: Recognize that skip is not free and scales with page depth.
hints: Ask how many rows the database touches to return page 5,000.
Consider why page one feels instant and page one thousand does not.
templates.explanation: The database cannot jump to row 100,000 — it reads and discards everything before it. Cursor pagination passes the last seen id and adds a where clause, letting the index seek directly to the position, which makes every page cost the same.

answerKey.flaw: Offset pagination makes the database walk and discard every skipped row, so cost grows linearly with how deep the user scrolls.
answerKey.consequence: Page 1 is instant and page 5,000 reads a hundred thousand rows to return twenty, so the feed degrades exactly for the most engaged users. Use a cursor on the ordering column instead of an offset.

weakAnswerSignals: Says an index fixes it without changing the query
Only suggests smaller pages
followUpPrompts: What do you pass to the client for a cursor to work?
mayaPushbacks: How does the database reach row 100,000?

templates.title: Borrowed and never returned
templates.prompt: This runs a report against a pooled connection. Explain what is wrong with it and what that costs in production.
templates.objective: Recognize an acquired resource released outside a finally.
hints: Trace what happens when the query throws.
Ask which line runs if an exception is raised above it.
templates.explanation: If query rejects, the exception propagates and release is never reached. The pool believes the connection is still in use and will not hand it out again. A handful of failures exhausts the pool, and the resulting outage looks like a database problem rather than a code problem.

answerKey.flaw: The connection is released only on the success path, so a query that throws leaks it out of the pool permanently.
answerKey.consequence: Every failing report removes one connection from the pool until the pool is empty and every request hangs waiting for one. Release in a finally block so it happens on both paths.

goodAnswerSignals: Names the leak on the error path
weakAnswerSignals: Says release is always called
Suggests only a larger pool
followUpPrompts: Why does this failure look like a database outage?
mayaPushbacks: What releases the connection when the query throws?

templates.title: Indexed, but not for this
templates.prompt: The comments table has an index on postId. This query is still slow. Explain why.
templates.objective: Recognize that an index must cover the filter and the ordering, not just one column.
hints: Ask what the database does after narrowing to one post.
Consider a post with fifty thousand comments.
templates.explanation: An index on postId narrows to one post, which may still be thousands of rows. The status filter and the createdAt sort both happen afterwards in memory. A composite index ordered to match the query lets the database walk the index in output order and stop at ten.

answerKey.flaw: The single-column index on postId cannot satisfy the status filter or the ordering, so the database sorts a large filtered set on every call.
answerKey.consequence: For a popular post the database reads every comment, filters by status and sorts them all to return ten rows. A composite index on (postId, status, createdAt desc) lets it seek and stop after ten.

goodAnswerSignals: Proposes a composite index covering filter and sort
weakAnswerSignals: Says the existing index is sufficient
Suggests caching without addressing the query
followUpPrompts: Why does the column order in a composite index matter?
mayaPushbacks: What does the index help with, and what is left over?

templates.title: Guarded on the client only
templates.prompt: The submit button is disabled after the first click. This is the handler behind it. Explain what is wrong.
templates.objective: Recognize a correctness guarantee enforced only where it cannot be trusted.
hints: Ask what happens if the browser retries after a timeout.
Consider a request sent from outside the browser entirely.
templates.explanation: A disabled button is a user experience improvement, not a guarantee. The server accepts any request it receives, including a retry after a timeout the client never saw succeed. Making the endpoint idempotent on a request key moves the guarantee to where it holds.

answerKey.flaw: Duplicate submissions are prevented only in the browser, so a retry, a refresh or a direct call creates a second order.
answerKey.consequence: Flaky networks, impatient refreshes and any non-browser client all produce duplicate orders that customers get charged for. Accept a client-supplied idempotency key and enforce it with a unique constraint.

goodAnswerSignals: Notices the server has no duplicate protection
weakAnswerSignals: Says the disabled button is sufficient
Suggests only rate limiting
followUpPrompts: Where should that key be generated?
mayaPushbacks: What stops a duplicate request that never came from your UI?

templates.title: Waiting inside the lock
templates.prompt: This charges a card and records the order together. Explain what is wrong with it and what that costs under load.
templates.objective: Recognize an external call widening a transaction far beyond database work.
hints: Ask how long the database locks are held for.
Consider what a rollback does about money already taken.
templates.explanation: A transaction should be as short as the writes it protects. Putting a network call inside means locks are held while waiting on a third party you do not control, and connection pool pressure follows. It also creates an inconsistency the transaction cannot fix: rolling back the rows does not refund the card.

answerKey.flaw: A slow external network call sits inside the database transaction, holding its locks for the whole duration of the payment.
answerKey.consequence: Row locks are held for hundreds of milliseconds per order, so under load transactions queue behind each other and the database becomes the bottleneck. Worse, a rollback cannot undo the charge. Move the external call outside the transaction.

goodAnswerSignals: Names the external call inside the transaction
Mentions lock duration or the unrollbackable charge
weakAnswerSignals: Says the transaction makes it safe
Suggests only a longer timeout
followUpPrompts: How would you restructure this so a rollback stays meaningful?
mayaPushbacks: Can the transaction roll back the payment?

templates.title: Optional all the way down
templates.prompt: This reads a value from an API response. Explain what is wrong with it.
templates.objective: Recognize defensive syntax that turns a missing structure into a plausible value.
hints: Ask how a broken response differs from a genuine zero here.
Consider what telemetry would show if the API changed shape.
templates.explanation: Each ?. quietly accepts an unexpected shape, and ?? 0 gives it a meaning. A response missing subscription entirely and a genuine zero-seat plan become indistinguishable, so a serialization bug or an outage looks like a business state. Validate the shape and treat a violation as an error.

answerKey.flaw: Optional chaining collapses a malformed or failed response into the same value as a legitimate zero, hiding the error.
answerKey.consequence: A broken API response silently downgrades a paying team to the free plan instead of surfacing a fault, and no telemetry records that the shape was wrong. Distinguish absent data from a real zero and fail loudly on the former.

goodAnswerSignals: Distinguishes missing data from a real zero
weakAnswerSignals: Praises the defensive chaining
Suggests more optional chaining
followUpPrompts: What should this do when subscription is absent?
mayaPushbacks: How would you find out the API changed shape?

templates.title: Exit before the flush
templates.prompt: This is a nightly job that reports its results to a metrics service. Explain what is wrong with it.
templates.objective: Recognize a forced exit discarding work that has been buffered but not sent.
hints: Ask whether the metrics call has actually been sent when exit runs.
Consider how a metrics client batches sends.
templates.explanation: process.exit does not wait for pending I/O. Most metrics clients batch over a short window, so a call made microseconds before exit never leaves the process. Awaiting an explicit flush, or simply returning and letting the event loop drain, delivers it.

answerKey.flaw: process.exit terminates immediately without letting the buffered metrics call flush, so the report is usually lost.
answerKey.consequence: The job succeeds but its telemetry never arrives, so dashboards show the job as never having run and a real failure is indistinguishable from a reporting gap. Await a flush, or let the process end naturally.

goodAnswerSignals: Proposes awaiting a flush or removing the exit
weakAnswerSignals: Says exit(0) is correct because the job succeeded
Focuses only on the exit code
followUpPrompts: Why might the process not exit on its own?
mayaPushbacks: Has the metric left the process when exit is called?

templates.title: Cached forever by accident
templates.prompt: This serves a user's private dashboard payload. Explain what is wrong with the response.
templates.objective: Recognize a caching directive whose scope does not match the data.
hints: Ask which caches are allowed to store a response marked public.
Note that the URL does not contain the user id.
templates.explanation: public tells every cache in the path that this response is shared. The URL does not vary by user — the identity comes from a session — so a proxy keyed on the URL alone will reuse it. private restricts storage to the end user's browser; no-store prevents caching altogether.

answerKey.flaw: Per-user private data is marked publicly cacheable, so shared caches may store it and serve one user's dashboard to another.
answerKey.consequence: A CDN or proxy can hand a cached response to a different user, leaking private data, and stale data persists for an hour after any change. Private per-user responses need private or no-store.

goodAnswerSignals: Identifies the public directive as wrong for per-user data
weakAnswerSignals: Says caching is always a performance win
Only suggests a shorter max-age
followUpPrompts: When would Vary be part of the answer here?
mayaPushbacks: Which cache decides this response can be reused?

templates.title: More than the client asked for
templates.prompt: This returns a profile to the browser. Explain what is wrong with it.
templates.objective: Recognize a response shape defined by the database rather than by the API.
hints: List every column this response contains today.
Ask what happens when someone adds a column to the users table.
templates.explanation: Passing the record straight to res.json couples the wire format to the table. Today it may only leak an internal flag; the real danger is that adding a column to the table silently adds it to the public response. An explicit projection makes exposure a deliberate act.

answerKey.flaw: The full database row is serialized directly, so every column including internal and sensitive fields is sent to the client.
answerKey.consequence: Password hashes, tokens, internal flags and anything a future migration adds are exposed the moment they exist, with no code change to notice. Serialize an explicit field list instead of the row.

templates.title: The whole file in memory
templates.prompt: This serves an export that users download. Explain what is wrong with it and what that costs.
templates.objective: Recognize a buffered read where a stream would do.
hints: Multiply the file size by the number of concurrent downloads.
Ask when the first byte reaches the user.
templates.explanation: readAll waits for the whole object before responding, so nothing is sent until everything is loaded and the peak memory is the full file per request. Streaming sends bytes as they arrive, keeps memory bounded by the chunk size, and lets the download start immediately.

answerKey.flaw: The entire object is read into memory before any bytes are sent, so memory use scales with file size times concurrent downloads.
answerKey.consequence: Ten users downloading a 500MB export need five gigabytes of resident memory, and the process is killed. Pipe the storage stream to the response so memory stays constant.

goodAnswerSignals: Ties memory to size times concurrency
weakAnswerSignals: Says it is fine for small files and stops there
Suggests only compression
followUpPrompts: What does streaming change about time-to-first-byte?
mayaPushbacks: What is the peak memory for ten concurrent downloads?

templates.title: Keyed by position
templates.prompt: This renders a reorderable list where each row holds its own input. Explain what is wrong with it.
templates.objective: Recognize an identity key that changes when the collection is reordered.
hints: Delete the first item mentally and follow where each component's state goes.
Ask what the key is supposed to identify.
templates.explanation: React uses the key to decide which component instance corresponds to which item across renders. An index says the second thing is the second thing, so removing an earlier entry shifts every subsequent item onto a different instance and inherits its state. A stable id keeps identity attached to data.

answerKey.flaw: Using the array index as the key ties component identity to position, so reordering or removing an item leaves state attached to the wrong row.
answerKey.consequence: Delete the first row and the text a user typed in it appears in the second, because React reuses the component at that index rather than the one for that item. Key by a stable item id.

goodAnswerSignals: Names the identity problem with index keys
Gives a reorder or delete example
weakAnswerSignals: Says index keys are fine because they are unique
Focuses only on the console warning
followUpPrompts: When is an index key genuinely acceptable?
mayaPushbacks: What does key identify — a position or an item?

templates.title: Midnight somewhere else
templates.prompt: This groups events into calendar days for a chart. Explain what is wrong with it.
templates.objective: Recognize a date calculation that silently assumes UTC.
hints: Work out which day 04:00 in Asia/Kolkata falls on under this function.
Ask which timezone toISOString renders in.
templates.explanation: toISOString always renders in UTC, so slicing the first ten characters gives the UTC calendar day. A day boundary is a local concept and differs from UTC by hours. Formatting in a chosen timezone, and being explicit about which one, is the only way the buckets match what the user experienced.

answerKey.flaw: Days are computed in UTC rather than the viewer's timezone, so events near midnight are counted on the wrong day.
answerKey.consequence: For a user in Asia/Kolkata, everything before 05:30 local is attributed to the previous day, so daily charts and streaks are wrong at exactly the hours users care about. Bucket in an explicit timezone.

weakAnswerSignals: Says ISO strings are timezone independent
Suggests only storing local time
followUpPrompts: Whose timezone should the buckets use, and where is it decided?
mayaPushbacks: Which timezone does toISOString use?

templates.title: A regex that hangs
templates.prompt: This validates a tag string from user input. Explain what is wrong with it.
templates.objective: Recognize a regular expression whose worst case is exponential in input length.
hints: Try a long run of word characters ending in a character that cannot match.
Ask how many ways the engine can split the input between the two quantifiers.
templates.explanation: Because \w+ and the surrounding group can both consume the same characters, the engine has many ways to divide the input. On a match it finds one quickly; on a failure it must try them all before rejecting. Since Node evaluates regexes synchronously, one request can stall every other one.

answerKey.flaw: The pattern nests a quantifier inside a quantified group, so a non-matching input causes catastrophic backtracking.
answerKey.consequence: A crafted string of thirty word characters followed by one invalid character makes the engine explore exponentially many splits, pinning a CPU core and blocking the event loop for the whole process. Rewrite the pattern without nested quantifiers.

goodAnswerSignals: Notes it blocks the whole event loop
weakAnswerSignals: Says the regex is correct so it is fine
Suggests only a length limit
followUpPrompts: How would you rewrite this without nested quantifiers?
mayaPushbacks: What does the engine do before it can report no match?

templates.title: Memoized on nothing
templates.prompt: This memoizes an expensive computation. Explain what is wrong with it.
templates.objective: Recognize a memo whose dependencies do not cover its inputs.
hints: List the values the callback reads, then compare them with the dependency array.
Ask what happens when the filter changes but the row count does not.
templates.explanation: useMemo recomputes only when a dependency changes. summarize reads both rows and filter, but the list mentions neither — only a derived length. Any change that keeps the count the same, including every filter change, returns the cached value. Dependencies must cover every input the callback reads.

answerKey.flaw: The dependency list watches only the row count, so the summary is not recomputed when filter changes or when rows change without changing length.
answerKey.consequence: Changing the filter leaves the previous summary on screen with no indication it is stale, and editing a row in place shows old numbers. Depend on the actual values the computation reads.

goodAnswerSignals: Notices filter is missing from the dependencies
weakAnswerSignals: Says rows.length is a valid proxy for rows
Suggests removing the memo without explaining
followUpPrompts: Why is rows.length tempting here, and why is it wrong?
mayaPushbacks: Which inputs does the callback read?
